newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: E.Asian Grain - Corn plunge not seen luring buyers.
newsitem.headline: E.Asian Grain - Corn plunge not seen luring buyers.

text.p: The sharp fall in U.S. corn prices to 14-month lows last week will not trigger immediate buying among East Asian buyers because it would be more than offset by a rise in freight rates, regional traders said on Monday.

Most buyers will also stay out of the market on expectations prices may slide further and to await the release of the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) crop report and world supply-demand estimates due out on November 12, they said.
"Our clients are not likely to move into the market at current levels until they become more confident that prices (have) fully bottomed," said a Seoul-based Japanese trader.
"They don't feel much need for hurry since they have already covered their needs till mid-1997 shipment," he said.
The Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) December corn futures contract fell on Friday to a fresh 14-month session low of US$2.62-1/2 a bushel. December closed three cents down at $2.63 a bushel.
"Most buyers are expected to remain on the sidelines at least until next Tuesday when the USDA releases the report," said a corn trader with the National Livestock Cooperatives Federation (NLCF).
The NLCF trader said the recent falls in corn prices were mostly offset by rises in freight rates.
"The freight premium to South Korean ports from the Pacific Northwest has risen to $14 per tonne from $12 two weeks ago, and from between $9 and $10 in late September," he added.
He said freight premiums from the U.S. Gulf to South Korea had also risen to $24 a tonne from between $21 and $22 a tonne two weeks ago.

In Japan, grain traders said they were also unlikely to buy much U.S. corn this week after covering most of their grain requirements for the January/March shipment period and would wait to see if prices will continue to fall.

"We bought U.S. corn actively when freight rates were firming last week," a corn trader at a major trade house said. "But at the moment, we'd like to watch and see if the CBOT will fall further before resuming buying."
Japanese importers have bought about 90 percent of their January/March requirement for U.S. corn, with premiums at 98 U.S. cents a bushel over the CBOT March futures contract.
Nearby freight rates on the U.S. Gulf/Japan grain route are currently quoted at about $22.50 a tonne.
Japanese importers have covered up to 80 percent of their U.S. soybean needs for December shipment with premiums at 130 U.S. cents a bushel over the CBOT January futures contract.
Regional traders said Taiwan may be the only market where buyers are likely to be tempted by the recent price falls.

Taiwan's Members Feed Industry Group bought 54,000 tonnes of corn at a tender on Friday while other organisations there may purchase up to 70,000 tonnes of corn and 156,000 tonnes of soybeans this week, the dealers said.

South Korea traders, in the meantime, said the domestic market appeared largely unaffected by fears of Karnal Bunt fungus hitting the U.S wheat crop or the resumption of the European Union's export subsidies.
Local buyers have shown little interest in EU wheat.
"We don't have much interest in the EU wheat market as long as U.S. wheat prices remain at a low level," one trader said.
Expectations of a bumper crop in Canada are also distracting local buyers from EU wheat, traders said.
In the Philippines, buyers were looking to buy more U.S. wheat if prices ease further this week, dealers said.
One Philippine company was also looking to buy up to 15,000 tonnes of soft wheat from Australia.
